item.prompt: Which sentence has a spelling error?
choices: Maya studied the plants in her science notebook before the big test today.
Leo raised his hand to give the right anwser to the teacher.
The path to the old barn runs straight through the tall cornfield.
Sam waited one more minute before he opened the gift.
item.correct_answer: Leo raised his hand to give the right anwser to the teacher.
item.spelling_pattern: silent w in answer: the s and w swapped

student_error.Maya studied the plants in her science n: science has a silent c after the s, so a student who expects 'sience' may think it is wrong
student_error.The path to the old barn runs straight t: straight has a silent gh, so the long spelling can look like an error
student_error.Sam waited one more minute before he ope: minute is said 'min-it', so a student may expect 'minit' and flag it

item.explanation: Answer has its silent w after the s (an-swer); anwser puts the w before the s. Science, straight and minute are all spelled correctly.

rated_no.option: Sam waited one more minute before he opened the gift.
reasons: all short, very familiar words; nothing to suspect
all short familiar words; nothing looks suspicious

item.prompt:
Which word correctly completes the sentence?

Every student will ____ a certificate at the end of the reading contest.
choices: recieve
receive
resieve
reseive
item.spelling_pattern: ei after c, and the soft c spelling the s sound
error_sites: -ei- written -ie-
c written s

student_error.recieve: applies 'i before e' without the 'except after c' part
student_error.reseive: spells the s sound with s instead of a soft c
student_error.resieve: writes the sound with s and then uses the ie order that usually follows s

item.explanation: Receive follows 'e before i after c': re-c-ei-ve. Recieve reverses the vowels, reseive uses s for c, and resieve does both.

reasons: replacing c with s and ie is not a form students write for this common word
s-for-c spelling; students have seen 'receive' with c
reseive is not a spelling students produce; they know the c
s-for-c spelling unlikely to look right

item.prompt: Which sentence has a spelling error?

Nora and her dad built a birdhouse for the backyard.
item.correct_answer: Lily heard a wierd noise coming from the attic.
item.spelling_pattern: ei exception: weird breaks 'i before e'

student_error.The store was very busy on the Saturday: busy is said 'bizzy', so the u can look like an error
student_error.Jack finished in fourth place in the sch: fourth has a u not heard in 'forth', so it may look like an extra letter
student_error.Nora and her dad built a birdhouse for t: built has a silent u, so a student expecting 'bilt' may flag it

item.explanation: Weird is an exception to 'i before e' and is spelled w-e-i-r-d; wierd reverses the vowels. Busy, fourth and built are spelled correctly.

rated_no.option: Nora and her dad built a birdhouse for the backyard.
reasons: simple compound words; nothing a student would flag
simple compound words, nothing looks wrong

item.spelling_pattern: y for the short i sound in the Greek prefix hypo-, and the unstressed e in -the-
error_sites: hy- written hi-
-the- written -thi-

student_error.hipothesis: spells the i sound in the first syllable with i, as it is heard
student_error.hypothisis: spells the unstressed vowel in -the- with i, matching the -sis ending
student_error.hipothisis: spells both unclear vowels with i

choices: You remembered to feed the fish before you left for school, Dani didn't you.
You remembered to feed the fish before you left for school, Dani didn't you?
You remembered to feed the fish before you left for school, Dani, didn't you.
You remembered to feed the fish before you left for school, Dani, didn't you?
item.correct_answer: You remembered to feed the fish before you left for school, Dani, didn't you?
error_sites: comma missing between the name in direct address and the tag question
period used instead of a question mark after the tag question

student_error.You remembered to feed the fish before y: runs the name into the tag and ends with a period because the sentence starts like a statement
puts a comma before the name but forgets the comma after it, so the name runs into the tag question
ends with a period because the sentence begins as a statement, not noticing the tag turns it into a question

item.explanation: A name used in direct address is set off with commas on both sides, so a comma is needed after 'Dani' as well as before it. A tag question such as 'didn't you' makes the whole sentence a question, so it ends with a question mark. Only the key has both.
item.punct_rule: commas around direct address before a tag question, and a question mark after the tag

rated_no.option: You remembered to feed the fish before you left for school, Dani didn't you.
reasons: no comma before tag and a question ending in a period; plainly wrong
missing the question mark and the comma; obviously off

choices: My grandmother (she turns eighty next month) still walks two miles every morning.
My grandmother, (she turns eighty next month) still walks two miles every morning.
My grandmother, (she turns eighty next month), still walks two miles every morning.
My grandmother (she turns eighty next month), still walks two miles every morning.
item.correct_answer: My grandmother (she turns eighty next month) still walks two miles every morning.
error_sites: extra comma before the opening parenthesis
extra comma after the closing parenthesis, between subject and verb

student_error.My grandmother, (she turns eighty next m: adds a comma before the parentheses as if setting off the extra information with commas too
uses commas and parentheses together, marking the extra information twice
student_error.My grandmother (she turns eighty next mo: adds a comma after the parenthesis where the reader pauses before the verb

item.explanation: Parentheses by themselves set off the extra information 'she turns eighty next month.' No comma goes before the opening parenthesis, and no comma goes after the closing one, because the sentence without the parenthetical, 'My grandmother still walks two miles every morning,' has no comma between subject and verb. Only the key has neither extra comma.
item.punct_rule: parentheses around a nonrestrictive element without added commas

rated_no.option: My grandmother, (she turns eighty next month) still walks two miles every morning.
reasons: comma before an opening parenthesis is not something students write

choices: On the first warm, spring morning, Hana wore her bright yellow rain boots to school.
On the first warm spring morning, Hana wore her bright yellow, rain boots to school.
On the first warm spring morning, Hana wore her bright yellow rain boots to school.
On the first warm, spring morning, Hana wore her bright yellow, rain boots to school.
item.correct_answer: On the first warm spring morning, Hana wore her bright yellow rain boots to school.
error_sites: extra comma between cumulative modifiers "warm" and "spring"
extra comma between cumulative modifiers "yellow" and "rain"

student_error.On the first warm, spring morning, Hana: puts a comma between any two describing words in a row without testing whether 'and' fits
student_error.On the first warm spring morning, Hana w: treats 'rain' as a separate adjective like 'yellow' instead of part of the noun 'rain boots'
student_error.On the first warm, spring morning, Hana: applies the coordinate-adjective comma to every string of modifiers

item.explanation: These modifiers are cumulative: 'warm and spring morning' and 'yellow and rain boots' make no sense, and the order cannot be reversed. 'Spring' and 'rain' work with the noun as a unit ('spring morning,' 'rain boots'). Cumulative modifiers take no comma between them, so only the key is correct.
item.punct_rule: no comma between cumulative adjectives or before a noun used as a modifier

rated_no.option: On the first warm spring morning, Hana wore her bright yellow, rain boots to school.
reasons: a comma splitting yellow from rain boots looks plainly wrong

rated_no.option: On the first warm, spring morning, Hana wore her bright yellow, rain boots to school.
reasons: two odd commas, including yellow, rain; unlikely

Our neighbor's loud, playful, golden retriever barks at every car that drives past.

extra comma between "playful" and the cumulative "golden" (part of "golden retriever")

student_error.Our neighbor's loud playful, golden retr: puts the single comma right before the color word instead of between the two adjectives that can be joined by 'and'

student_error.Our neighbor's loud, playful, golden ret: puts a comma after every adjective, as in a list

item.punct_rule: in a mixed string, a comma only between the coordinate pair and none before the cumulative modifier

rated_no.option: Our neighbor's loud playful, golden retriever barks at every car that drives past.
reasons: comma placed after playful before golden makes no sense to students

Either Marcus nor his older sisters is going to walk the dog after dinner tonight.
Either Marcus nor his older sisters are going to walk the dog after dinner tonight.
Either Marcus or his older sisters are going to walk the dog after dinner tonight.
item.correct_answer: Either Marcus or his older sisters are going to walk the dog after dinner tonight.
error_sites: "nor" used with "either" instead of "or"
singular verb "is" used though the nearer subject "sisters" is plural

student_error.Either Marcus or his older sisters is go: makes the verb agree with the first subject, 'Marcus,' instead of the nearer subject, 'sisters'
student_error.Either Marcus nor his older sisters is g: mixes up the either/or and neither/nor pairs and agrees the verb with 'Marcus'

item.explanation: The correlative pair is 'either...or'; 'nor' belongs with 'neither.' When two subjects are joined by 'either...or,' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, here the plural 'sisters,' so 'are' is correct. Only the key uses 'or' and 'are.'
item.varied_dimension: correlative conjunction pair; verb agreement with the nearer of two subjects

reasons: either...nor is a pairing students do not write

error_sites: present-tense "rides" shifts out of the past tense in the series of verbs
present-tense "meets" shifts out of the past tense in the later clause

student_error.Last Saturday, Jonah woke up early, pack: keeps the main verbs in the past but slips into present tense in the clause at the end, far from 'Last Saturday'

item.map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: Because the trail was steep and rocky, we reached the top before noon even though we had started hiking at dawn.
Although the trail was steep and rocky, we reached the top before noon since we had started hiking at dawn.
Because the trail was steep and rocky, we reached the top before noon since we had started hiking at dawn.
Although the trail was steep and rocky, we reached the top before noon even though we had started hiking at dawn.
item.correct_answer: Although the trail was steep and rocky, we reached the top before noon since we had started hiking at dawn.
error_sites: "Because" signals cause where the opening clause states a contrast
"even though" signals contrast where the closing clause gives the cause

student_error.Because the trail was steep and rocky, w: picks a subordinating conjunction for each clause without checking how that clause relates to the main idea
starts with 'Because' out of habit, without noticing a steep trail would slow the hikers down rather than help
student_error.Although the trail was steep and rocky,: repeats the contrast idea from the opening clause instead of seeing that starting early explains the early arrival

item.explanation: A steep, rocky trail would make the hike slower, so reaching the top early happened in spite of it: 'Although' signals that contrast. Starting at dawn is the reason the hikers arrived before noon, so a cause conjunction such as 'since' is needed. Only the key signals both relationships correctly.
item.varied_dimension: contrast conjunction in the opening dependent clause; cause conjunction in the closing dependent clause

rated_no.option: Because the trail was steep and rocky, we reached the top before noon even though we had started hiking at dawn.
reasons: because steep, we reached it early contradicts itself; even weak readers notice

Having grew up on a farm, Mateo was used to wake up before sunrise.
Having grown up on a farm, Mateo was used to waking up before sunrise.
Having grew up on a farm, Mateo was used to waking up before sunrise.
item.correct_answer: Having grown up on a farm, Mateo was used to waking up before sunrise.
error_sites: simple past "grew" used instead of the past participle "grown" in the perfect participial phrase
base verb "wake" used instead of the gerund "waking" after "was used to"

student_error.Having grown up on a farm, Mateo was use: confuses 'was used to' (accustomed to, followed by a gerund) with 'used to' (habit, followed by a base verb)
student_error.Having grew up on a farm, Mateo was used: does not recognize either verbal: uses the simple past after 'Having' and treats 'to' as part of an infinitive
uses the simple past 'grew' after 'Having' instead of the past participle

item.explanation: A perfect participle is 'having' plus the past participle, so 'Having grown' is correct. In 'was used to' (meaning 'was accustomed to'), 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by a gerund: 'waking up.' Only the key uses both verbal forms correctly.
item.varied_dimension: past participle in a perfect participial phrase; gerund after 'be used to'

rated_no.option: Having grew up on a farm, Mateo was used to wake up before sunrise.
reasons: having grew plus used to wake; two plain errors students rarely accept

item.map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: If Carmen would have left home ten minutes earlier, she had caught the bus to the game.
If Carmen had left home ten minutes earlier, she had caught the bus to the game.
If Carmen would have left home ten minutes earlier, she would have caught the bus to the game.
If Carmen had left home ten minutes earlier, she would have caught the bus to the game.
item.correct_answer: If Carmen had left home ten minutes earlier, she would have caught the bus to the game.
error_sites: "would have left" used in the if-clause of a past contrary-to-fact conditional instead of "had left"
"had caught" used in the result clause instead of the conditional "would have caught"

student_error.If Carmen would have left home ten minut: swaps the two verb forms, putting 'would have' in the if-clause and 'had' in the result clause
student_error.If Carmen had left home ten minutes earl: uses the same past perfect form in both clauses to keep the tenses matching
student_error.If Carmen would have left home ten minut: uses 'would have' in both clauses, as is common in speech

item.explanation: For an imagined past situation that did not happen, the if-clause uses the past perfect ('had left') and the result clause uses 'would have' plus the past participle ('would have caught'). 'Would have' does not belong in the if-clause, and 'had caught' states a fact rather than an imagined result. Only the key uses the conditional mood correctly in both clauses.
item.varied_dimension: conditional mood in the if-clause; conditional mood in the result clause

rated_no.option: If Carmen would have left home ten minutes earlier, she had caught the bus to the game.
reasons: had caught in the result clause plus would have in the if-clause; reads wrong
'had caught' in result clause plus 'would have' in if-clause; reads wrong
